set1.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: Who is credited with developing the first computed tomography scanner, and what recognition followed?
opts: Sir Godfrey Hounsfield, who won the 1979 Nobel Prize in Medicine along with Allan Cormack
Correct — the unit of attenuation is named after him.
Wilhelm Roentgen, who won the first Nobel Prize for Physics in 1901
He discovered x-rays rather than computed tomography.
Allan Cormack alone, who won the 1979 Nobel Prize for Physics
He shared the 1979 Medicine prize with Hounsfield.
Paul Lauterbur, who won the Nobel Prize for developing magnetic resonance imaging
That work was on magnetic resonance rather than computed tomography.

set1.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: What does fluoroscopy allow that a conventional radiograph does not?
opts: Real-time visualisation, allowing evaluation of motion and of positional change in bones and joints
Correct — images can be viewed live and captured as stills or video.
Imaging without any ionizing radiation at all, making it entirely safe to use in pregnancy
Fluoroscopy does use ionizing radiation.
Cross-sectional imaging in any geometric plane after acquisition
That describes computed tomography.
Differentiation of soft tissues superior to computed tomography
That describes magnetic resonance imaging.

set1.io: Objective e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set1.q: What are the midsagittal and parasagittal planes?
opts: Midsagittal runs across the shoulders; parasagittal sections lie anterior and posterior
That division is coronal rather than sagittal.
Midsagittal runs at the level of the heart; parasagittal sections are angled off the axis
The distinction is position relative to the midline, not level or angle.
Midsagittal runs in the body's midline; parasagittal sections lie to either side of it
Correct — the midsagittal plane is also called the median plane.
Midsagittal runs through the umbilicus; parasagittal sections lie above and below it
Both sagittal planes are vertical and separate right from left, not upper from lower.

set1.io: Objective i — Discuss the importance of communication between the physician assistant and radiology team
set1.q: What should you do if you are unsure which modality to order?
opts: Order both the plain film and the cross-sectional study at the same visit
Ordering in parallel is not what the deck recommends for uncertainty.
Tell the radiologist what you are looking for, and they can guide the choice
Correct — the question you are asking is the useful thing to communicate.
Order the study with the widest range of densities, and narrow down afterwards
Defaulting to the broadest study is not the advice the deck gives.
Order the study with the lowest radiation dose, and escalate only if it is negative
Dose matters in the diagnostic approach, but this is not the stated advice.

set1.io: Objective h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set1.q: What does the deck give as the key takeaway on contrast safety?
opts: Always obtain written consent and give a prophylactic antihistamine
Neither of these is stated as the takeaway for contrast administration.
Always ask about allergies and assess kidney function
Correct — and pre-treatment exists when contrast is absolutely necessary.
Always withhold contrast when any drug allergy is documented
Pre-treatment is available, so a documented allergy is not an absolute bar.
Always use the iso-osmolal agent regardless of the indication or the patient
Iodixanol is believed safer but is not mandated for every study.

set1.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: Which advantages are named for computed tomography?
opts: It expands the grey scale beyond the five basic densities, reduces overlapping of structures, works with implantable devices, and allows three-dimensional reconstruction
Correct — it is described as the cornerstone of cross-sectional imaging.
It uses no ionizing radiation at all and is described as being the safest of all of the imaging modalities that are currently available anywhere
That describes ultrasound.
It is fully portable, inexpensive, and can be brought to the patient's bedside
It is described as not truly portable.
It is superior to magnetic resonance imaging for differentiating soft tissues
Magnetic resonance imaging is superior for soft tissue.

set1.io: Objective h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set1.q: How does the deck summarise ultrasound's safety?
opts: Safe once screened, though implanted metallic devices must be excluded beforehand
Implanted-device screening is a magnetic resonance requirement.
Very safe, without any known major side effects at medically diagnostic levels
Correct — it is called the safest of these modalities.
Broadly safe, though a cumulative dose limit applies across repeated examinations
There is no cumulative dose, because there is no ionizing radiation.
Safe in adults, though it is avoided in pregnancy and in infants as a precaution
That caution is stated for magnetic resonance imaging, not for ultrasound.

set1.io: Objective h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set1.q: What does the deck say about shellfish allergy and iodinated contrast?
opts: There should be no cross-reactivity between shellfish and iodinated radiocontrast
Correct — the cross-reactivity idea is explicitly rejected.
There is well-established cross-reactivity, so the two allergies must be treated as one
This is the belief the deck corrects rather than the position it takes.
There is partial cross-reactivity, so contrast may be given at a reduced concentration
No such graded approach is described; the cross-reactivity itself is denied.
There is cross-reactivity only with the iso-osmolal agents such as iodixanol
The deck draws no agent-specific exception of this kind.

set1.io: Objective g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set1.q: What are technetium-99's stated indications, and how does it distribute?
opts: Bone scans, myocardial perfusion, functional brain imaging, immunoscintigraphy and sentinel node identification; it travels to areas of higher blood flow and cellular activity
Correct — a white blood cell uptake scan is also named.
Cancer staging, brain disorders and cardiac blood flow, together with tumour delineation and lesion characterisation; it concentrates wherever the glucose consumption of the tissue is highest
Glucose consumption describes fluorodeoxyglucose in positron emission tomography.
Vasculopathy, emboli, thrombi, stenosis and aneurysm assessment, along with graft surveillance; it fills the vascular lumen and is imaged during the first pass through it
Luminal filling on a first pass describes iodinated angiographic contrast.
Central nervous system tumours, metastases and soft tissue masses; it shortens relaxation times in the tissue it reaches
Altering relaxation times is how gadolinium works in magnetic resonance.

set1.io: Objective c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set1.q: Which programmable magnetic resonance technique is named as useful in stroke?
opts: Fat-suppressed imaging, which removes the signal from adipose tissue in the field
Fat suppression is not the technique the deck names for stroke.
Post-processing windowing, which re-displays the raw data over a narrower range
Post-processing and windowing are computed tomography techniques.
Gadolinium-enhanced imaging, which highlights vascular structures after injection
Contrast enhancement is used for tumours and masses rather than for stroke here.
Diffusion-weighted imaging, which evaluates the diffusion of water within tissue
Correct — the scanner can also be programmed to evaluate blood velocity.

set1.io: Objective e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set1.q: How are patients positioned for ultrasound examinations?
opts: A single standardised position for every study, with the transducer angle changed instead
The deck describes dozens of potential positions rather than one standard.
Standing for all abdominal work and seated for all cardiac work, without exception
No such rigid division is described, and most patients are some form of supine.
Prone for all studies, so that the transducer can be applied along the posterior surface
Prone is not the usual ultrasound position described here.
Dozens of positions depending on the structure and the complaint, most often some form of supine
Correct — head position varies, and the position follows what is being examined.

set1.io: Objective e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set1.q: How are radiographic projections named?
opts: In the direction the patient faces, from the side nearest the film to the side furthest away
The naming follows the beam rather than which way the patient is turned.
In the order the structures appear, from the most superficial down to the deepest tissue
Projections are not named for the order in which structures are encountered on the image.
In the position of the detector, from the cassette's near edge to its furthest corner
The detector's own geometry does not supply the name of the projection.
In the direction the beam travels, from what it strikes first to the most distal portion
Correct — so posterior-anterior means the beam enters the back and exits the front.

set1.io: Objective f — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with radiation exposure
set1.q: Which imaging devices does the deck flag as the highest-emitting currently in existence?
opts: Computed tomography, positron emission tomography and single photon emission tomography
Correct — the deck marks this IMPORTANT, and all three use ionizing radiation.
Conventional radiography, fluoroscopy and the angiographic studies performed with x-rays
These do use ionizing radiation, but the deck calls plain films relatively low dose.
Magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography and magnetic resonance venography
None of the magnetic resonance studies emit ionizing radiation at all.
Ultrasonography, colour Doppler ultrasonography and the hand-held bedside ultrasound units
Ultrasound uses sound waves and is called the safest of these modalities.

set1.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set1.q: Which density is described as the most dense naturally occurring material?
opts: Fluid
Fluid and soft tissue share a middle density.
Fat
Fat is less dense than soft tissue.
Calcium
Correct — it absorbs most x-rays, though metal absorbs essentially all of them.
Metal
Metal is denser but is not naturally occurring in the body.

set1.io: Objective g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set1.q: Which agent is used for fluoroscopic swallow studies, and how is the study performed?
opts: Oral gadolinium, with sequential magnetic resonance images taken as the patient swallows
Gadolinium is intravenous and belongs to magnetic resonance, not fluoroscopy.
Intravenous iohexol, with sequential computed tomography images taken during swallowing
An intravascular agent does not opacify the swallowed bolus.
Oral technetium, with sequential gamma camera images taken as the patient swallows
Technetium is a nuclear medicine tracer rather than a swallow-study agent.
Oral barium, with sequential x-rays taken as the patient swallows it
Correct — real-time imaging is what makes fluoroscopy suit a swallow study.

set1.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set1.q: Which two of the five basic densities cannot be distinguished from one another on a conventional radiograph?
opts: Calcium and metal, which both absorb all of the beam
Metal usually absorbs all x-rays while calcium absorbs most; they are distinguishable.
Fat and calcium, which occupy adjacent points on the scale
They sit at opposite ends of the middle range and are distinguishable.
Fluid and soft tissue, which have the same density
Correct — that limitation is one reason computed tomography expands the grey scale.
Fat and air, which both appear black on the image
Fat is grey and somewhat darker than soft tissue, while air is blackest.

set1.io: Objective a — Identify the fundamental properties of medical imaging
set1.q: Who discovered x-rays, and what recognition followed?
opts: Allan Cormack, in South Africa in 1963, awarded the first Nobel Prize for Physics
He shared the 1979 Medicine prize for computed tomography.
Marie Curie, in France in 1898, awarded the Nobel Prize for Physics in 1903
Her work was on radioactivity rather than the discovery of x-rays.
Wilhelm Roentgen, in Germany in 1895, awarded the first Nobel Prize for Physics in 1901
Correct — the technique is still called roentgenography after him.
Godfrey Hounsfield, in Britain in 1972, awarded the Nobel Prize for Medicine in 1979
He developed the first computed tomography scanner, with Allan Cormack.

set1.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set1.q: What do the terms radiolucent and hypodense describe?
opts: A region of increased uptake of an injected radioisotope on nuclear imaging
That terminology belongs to nuclear medicine.
A darker image, from greater passage of x-ray photons through the tissue and therefore less absorption
Correct — radiopaque and hyperdense describe the opposite.
A whiter image, from less passage of x-ray photons through the tissue and therefore greater absorption
That describes radiopaque or hyperdense tissue.
A brighter signal on a T2-weighted magnetic resonance image of the same tissue
That terminology belongs to magnetic resonance imaging.

set1.io: Objective e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set1.q: What does the deck call the most important thing to remember about ultrasound orientation?
opts: Which frequency is selected: high for superficial structures, low for deeper structures
Transducer frequency is a resolution and penetration trade-off, not orientation.
Where the indicator is: on the right of the screen in cardiac imaging, on the left for everything else
Correct — it is called crucial, because the whole image flips with it.
Where the indicator is: on the left of the screen in cardiac imaging, on the right for everything else
This reverses the convention the deck gives for the heart.
How deep the focus is set: shallow for superficial structures, deep for abdominal structures
Focal depth matters for image quality but is not the orientation rule stated.

set1.io: Objective c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set1.q: What does an abdominal series evaluate, and how is the patient positioned?
opts: The gastrointestinal tract, with the patient standing, to assess air-fluid levels or free air
Correct — upright is what makes free air and air-fluid levels visible.
The genitourinary tract, with the patient supine, to assess stones within the collecting system
Supine and urinary describes the kidney-ureter-bladder film instead.
The gastrointestinal tract, with the patient supine, to assess bowel wall thickness and oedema
The series is shot standing, and wall thickness is not what it is described as assessing.
The retroperitoneum, with the patient in decubitus, to assess the psoas shadows and the flanks
Decubitus positioning is described for pleural effusion, not for this study.

set1.io: Objective g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set1.q: Which agent is named for intravenous contrast in computed tomography, and what is it?
opts: Visipaque (iodixanol), a barium salt suspension given into the vein
Iodixanol is iodinated and iso-osmolal; barium is enteral and never intravenous.
Gadolinium, a paramagnetic metal chelate given into the vein
Gadolinium is the magnetic resonance agent, not the computed tomography one.
Gastrografin, a water-soluble iodinated agent given into the vein
Gastrografin is an oral agent used when perforation is suspected.
Omnipaque (iohexol), a radioactive form of iodine given into the vein
Correct — the same agent is used, at higher concentration, for angiography.

set1.io: Objective g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set1.q: Which vascular magnetic resonance studies are performed without contrast?
opts: Coronary angiography and retrograde pyelography
Both of these are performed with injected contrast material.
Arthrography and intrathecal myelography
Both are defined by contrast being injected into a space.
Magnetic resonance angiography and magnetic resonance venography
Correct — both are done without a contrast agent.
Computed tomography angiography and computed tomography venography
The computed tomography vascular studies do require an iodinated injection.

set1.io: Objective c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set1.q: Which tissues is magnetic resonance imaging described as the best modality for?
opts: Metabolically active tissue, essentially tumour and infection, with high functional detail
Metabolic activity is what the nuclear medicine studies are indicated for.
Soft tissue, essentially anything other than bone, with extremely high anatomical detail
Correct — the deck states it in exactly those terms.
Bone and calcified structures, essentially anything mineralised, with high spatial detail
Calcium emits no signal on magnetic resonance, which is the opposite of this claim.
Air-containing structures, essentially the lungs and sinuses, with high contrast detail
Aerated structures are a radiographic and tomographic strength, not this one.

set1.io: Objective c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set1.q: What does a kidney-ureter-bladder film evaluate, and how is the patient positioned?
opts: The genitourinary tract, with the patient supine and the film shot anterior-posterior
Correct — supine and anterior-posterior distinguishes it from the abdominal series.
The gastrointestinal tract, with the patient standing and the film shot anterior-posterior
Standing and anterior-posterior describes the abdominal series, which assesses bowel.
The genitourinary tract, with the patient standing and the film shot posterior-anterior
The kidney-ureter-bladder film is taken supine, not upright.
The gastrointestinal tract, with the patient supine and the film shot posterior-anterior
Both halves are wrong: it is a urinary study and it is an anterior-posterior film.

set1.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set1.q: What does increased attenuation mean on a computed tomography image, and how does it appear?
opts: A substance producing no signal at all, appearing as a signal void
That describes calcium on magnetic resonance imaging.
A region taking up more injected radioisotope than surrounding tissue
That describes uptake on nuclear imaging.
A denser substance with a high computed tomography number, appearing whiter
Correct — the same substances would be radiopaque on a conventional radiograph.
A less dense substance with a low computed tomography number, appearing blacker
That describes decreased attenuation.

set1.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: Which term names an angiographic study of the veins rather than the arteries?
opts: Doppler study, performed as either a colour Doppler examination or a duplex examination
Colour Doppler shows flow in either vessel type; it is not the venous-specific term.
Coronary angiogram, performed as either a diagnostic catheterisation or an intervention
The coronary angiogram is the x-ray-based arterial study of the heart.
Arthrogram, performed as either a computed tomography arthrogram or a magnetic one
An arthrogram is contrast injected into a joint, not a vascular study at all.
Venogram, performed as either a magnetic resonance venogram or a computed tomography venogram
Correct — the same modalities, aimed at the venous side.

set1.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: How is a conventional radiograph produced?
opts: A magnetic field aligns hydrogen atoms, which emit radio waves when the field is released
That describes magnetic resonance imaging.
A gamma camera detects photons emitted by an injected radioisotope within the patient
That describes nuclear medicine imaging.
Ionizing radiation and light strike a photosensitive surface, producing a latent image that is then processed to become visible
Correct — it requires a source, a method to record the image, and a way to process it.
High-frequency sound waves bounce off the tissue and return to a transducer, which then builds up the whole image
That describes ultrasound.

set1.io: Objective c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set1.q: In which patients is ultrasound named as often the first study of choice?
opts: Adult chest and geriatric patients, and it is also used to screen for fractures
Air in the lung and bone both defeat ultrasound; these are radiographic studies.
Head-injured and intoxicated patients, and it is also used to exclude a bleed
Intracranial haemorrhage is a computed tomography question in the adult skull.
Oncology and post-operative patients, and it is also used to stage known disease
Staging is a computed tomography and positron emission tomography role.
Female pelvis and paediatric patients, and it is also used to guide procedures
Correct — no radiation is the reason it leads in both groups.

set1.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set1.q: How does ultrasonography generate an image?
opts: High-metabolism tissues concentrate injected tracer, which emits gamma radiation
That is nuclear medicine, and it requires an injected radioactive agent.
High-frequency sound waves leave the transducer, bounce off tissue and return to it
Correct — the transducer is both the source and the receiver.
High-energy x-ray photons leave the tube, pass through tissue and strike a detector
That is radiography; ultrasound uses no ionizing radiation whatsoever.
High-strength magnetic fields align hydrogen, which emits radio waves on release
That is magnetic resonance imaging, which images hydrogen rather than sound.

set1.io: Objective h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set1.q: What are the stated risks of fluorodeoxyglucose-18?
opts: Frequent anaphylaxis requiring pre-treatment, and it may cause hyperglycaemia
Allergic reactions to the nuclear medicine agents are described as rare.
No contraindications and no known nephrotoxicity, though it may cause hyperglycaemia
Correct — it is renally cleared, so the urinary tract is always contrast positive.
No contraindications and no known nephrotoxicity, though it may cause hypoglycaemia
The agent is a glucose analogue; the effect named is a rise, not a fall.
Significant nephrotoxicity requiring pre-hydration, and it may cause hyperglycaemia
Pre-hydration and nephrotoxicity belong to iodinated contrast instead.

set2.io: Objective i — Discuss the importance of communication between the physician assistant and radiology team
set2.q: What practical ordering point does the deck make about imaging several body regions?
opts: Multiple body parts should be combined into one single order, so that the patient is scanned once and the radiologist reads the whole study together
The deck makes the opposite point about how these studies are requested.
Multiple body parts require the radiologist to countersign the request before booking
No countersignature requirement is described.
Multiple body parts must be imaged on separate days to limit cumulative radiation dose
Magnetic resonance emits no ionizing radiation, and no such rule is stated.
Multiple body parts or sections may mean multiple orders, giving brain, cervical, thoracic and lumbar spine as the example
Correct — one clinical question can require four separate requests.

set2.io: Objective e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set2.q: How are patients usually positioned for computed tomography, nuclear medicine and magnetic resonance studies?
opts: Supine, and the images are traditionally acquired in transverse sections
Correct — supine is the standard across all three of these.
Standing, and the images are traditionally acquired in coronal sections
Upright positioning belongs to the abdominal series and the chest radiograph.
Decubitus, and the images are traditionally acquired in sagittal sections
Decubitus is a plain-film position used to look for layering pleural fluid.
Prone, and the images are traditionally acquired in oblique sections
Prone is not the standard position described for these scanners.

set2.io: Objective e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set2.q: Why is the posterior-anterior chest view preferred over the anterior-posterior view?
opts: It reduces magnification of the heart, so cardiomegaly is not misread, and it lowers dose to radiation-sensitive organs
Correct — the heart sits anteriorly, so it is closer to the detector on this view.
It reduces magnification of the lungs, so effusion is not missed, and it raises dose to less sensitive posterior tissue
Magnification affects the heart, and no view is preferred for raising dose anywhere.
It shortens the exposure time needed, so motion blur is reduced, and it removes the need for a lateral view
The deck notes these views are typically still combined with a lateral.
It removes overlap of the ribs entirely, so fractures are easier to see, and it avoids the need for oblique views
Posterior ribs are better visualised, but overlap is not removed entirely.

set2.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: What does the colour Doppler setting add to a standard ultrasound image?
opts: Depth of penetration and resolution, on an image otherwise limited to superficial planes
Colour Doppler does not extend depth; poor deep visualisation remains a limitation.
Density in Hounsfield units and windowing, on an image otherwise showing five densities
Hounsfield units and windowing belong to computed tomography, not to ultrasound.
Metabolic uptake and intensity, on an image otherwise showing only anatomical structure
Uptake displayed by intensity is how the positron emission studies are read.
Direction of flow and velocity, on an image otherwise made of white, grey and black
Correct — colour is the flow overlay, and blood is what it is used for.

set2.io: Objective h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set2.q: What is the stated safety record of technetium-99?
opts: Allergic reactions are rare, and no organ damage has previously been documented
Correct — neither nephrotoxicity nor hepatotoxicity is documented.
Allergic reactions are common, though no organ damage has previously been documented
The deck describes allergic reactions as rare rather than common.
Allergic reactions are rare, though documented nephrotoxicity requires pre-hydration
No nephrotoxicity has been documented for this agent.
Allergic reactions are rare, though documented hepatotoxicity requires liver monitoring
Hepatotoxicity is specifically listed as not documented.

set2.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: Which substance is assigned a Hounsfield number of zero by convention?
opts: Bone
Bone sits at the high, positive end of the scale.
Fat
Fat sits below water on the scale but is not the zero reference.
Water
Correct — other tissues take a range of Hounsfield numbers according to their density.
Air
Air sits at the low, negative end of the scale.

set2.io: Objective e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set2.q: Beyond the heart, what else is better seen on the posterior-anterior chest view?
opts: Maximum visualisation of the mediastinum, better visualisation of the hila, and well visualised anterior ribs
The deck names the lung fields, apices and posterior ribs rather than these.
Maximum visualisation of the diaphragm, better visualisation of free air, and well visualised gastric bubble
Free air beneath the diaphragm is what an upright abdominal series is for.
Maximum visualisation of the pleura, better visualisation of layering fluid, and well visualised costophrenic angles
Layering fluid with gravity is the decubitus view's stated purpose.
Maximum visualisation of the lung, better visualisation of the apices, and well visualised posterior ribs
Correct — all three are listed alongside the cardiac and dose advantages.

set2.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set2.q: Which term describes tissue that appears white because it absorbs more of the beam?
opts: Radiopaque, also called hyperdense or radiodense
Correct — less passage of x-ray photons produces the whiter appearance.
Radiolucent, also called hypodense
That describes darker tissue with greater photon passage.
Isodense, matching the density of the surrounding tissue
That term is not the one for a white appearance.
Attenuated, meaning the beam has been scattered away
Increased attenuation is a computed tomography term for the same idea.

set2.io: Objective e — Discuss the importance of patient positioning in medical imaging
set2.q: Which three standard planes are used in cross-sectional imaging, and how does each divide the body?
opts: Axial into right and left, coronal into upper and lower, sagittal into anterior and posterior
This rotates all three assignments and is wrong on each one.
Axial into upper and lower, coronal into right and left, sagittal into anterior and posterior
Coronal and sagittal are swapped; coronal separates front from back.
Axial into upper and lower, coronal into anterior and posterior, sagittal into right and left
Correct — axial is also called transverse and is the commonest of the three.
Axial into anterior and posterior, coronal into right and left, sagittal into upper and lower
Each plane here is matched to the wrong division of the body.

set2.io: Objective g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set2.q: Into which spaces can contrast be injected, and what is each study called?
opts: Muscle for a myogram, the pleural space directly, and the ureter for an antegrade pyelogram
None of these three routes is described in the deck.
Bowel for an arthrogram, the epidural space, and the renal pelvis for a cystogram
The names are attached to the wrong spaces throughout.
Joints for an arthrogram, the central nervous system intrathecally, and the bladder for a retrograde pyelogram
Correct — three routes named besides the intravascular and enteral ones.
Joints for a venogram, the central nervous system intravenously, and the bladder for a cystogram
A venogram images veins, and intrathecal is the route named for the nervous system.

set2.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: What are ultrasonography's stated indications?
opts: Assessment of aerated structures, naming the lungs, the sinuses and the bowel gas pattern
Large gas-filled structures disrupt the signal, which is a stated limitation.
Assessment of metabolic activity, naming tumour staging, brain function and perfusion
Metabolic activity is what the nuclear medicine studies are indicated for.
Assessment of moving structures, naming the heart, the vasculature and obstetrics
Correct — it records in real time, which is what suits it to motion.
Assessment of bony structures, naming the skull, the vertebrae and the long bones
Ultrasound cannot penetrate bone, so these are radiographic or tomographic studies.

set2.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set2.q: Which substances show decreased attenuation on computed tomography?
opts: Metal and calcium, which absorb more x-rays and appear whiter
Those show increased attenuation.
Fluid and soft tissue, which sit at exactly zero Hounsfield units
Water is zero by convention; soft tissue takes a range above it.
Gadolinium and iodine, which are used as contrast agents
Contrast agents increase attenuation where they collect.
Air and fat, which absorb fewer x-rays and appear blacker
Correct — on a conventional radiograph they would show decreased density or increased lucency.

set2.io: Objective g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set2.q: What are the named indications for intravenous contrast in computed tomography?
opts: Inflammation, cancer staging, tumour delineation, vasculopathy, emboli, thrombi, stenosis and aneurysms
Correct — the vascular indications and the oncological ones are listed together.
Fracture, dislocation, foreign body, joint effusion, bone tumour, osteomyelitis and arthritis
Musculoskeletal indications of this kind are not what contrast is listed for.
Stroke, demyelination, cord compression, disc herniation, meningitis and hydrocephalus
Central nervous system tumour characterisation is listed under magnetic resonance.
Pneumonia, effusion, pneumothorax, atelectasis, emphysema and interstitial lung disease
These parenchymal lung findings are not the contrast indications named.

set2.io: Objective g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set2.q: What is oral contrast indicated for?
opts: Structure or disease of the urinary space, anywhere from the renal pelvis to the urethra
The urinary tract is imaged with an injected or retrograde agent instead.
Structure or disease of the intraluminal space, anywhere from the upper oesophagus to the rectum
Correct — it outlines the lumen of the gastrointestinal tract.
Structure or disease of the vascular space, anywhere from the aortic root to the digital arteries
Vascular imaging requires an intravascular injection, not an oral agent.
Structure or disease of the pleural space, anywhere from the apex to the costophrenic angle
Oral contrast does not reach the pleural space.

set2.io: Objective f — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with radiation exposure
set2.q: In which units is radiation measured?
opts: Hertz and decibels
Those describe sound waves in ultrasound.
Millisieverts and milligrays
Correct — x-ray radiation is low compared with other radiographic modalities.
Hounsfield units and pixels
Hounsfield units measure computed tomography attenuation rather than radiation dose.
Tesla and gauss
Those measure magnetic field strength in magnetic resonance imaging.

set2.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: What is post-processing, and what does it avoid?
opts: Reformatting the printed film after it has been developed, in order to improve the contrast that is seen on the hard copy
The benefit described is digital rather than photographic.
Giving a second dose of contrast to improve the visibility of a lesion
Post-processing specifically avoids re-exposing the patient.
Repeating the scan at a different slice thickness to improve resolution
Post-processing specifically avoids repeating the study.
Manipulating the raw data after acquisition to best demonstrate an abnormality, without repeating the study or re-exposing the patient
Correct — digital imaging markedly advanced this ability.

set2.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set2.q: Which density appears blackest on a conventional radiograph, and why?
opts: Metal, because it absorbs the most x-rays of any material
Metal usually absorbs all x-rays and appears whitest.
Calcium, because it is the densest naturally occurring material
Calcium absorbs most x-rays and appears near-white.
Fat, because it is less dense than the surrounding soft tissue
Fat is grey and somewhat darker than soft tissue, but not blackest.
Air, because it absorbs the least x-rays
Correct — greater passage of photons means a darker image.

set2.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: How are magnetic resonance images generated?
opts: A pulse of sound leaves the transducer; the echo returning from tissue is timed and plotted
That is ultrasonography, and it needs no magnetic field of any kind.
A varying magnetic field aligns hydrogen atoms; releasing it produces radio waves the computer maps
Correct — the deck calls the resulting images essentially hydrogen maps.
A varying magnetic field aligns iron atoms; releasing it produces heat the computer measures
Hydrogen is the nucleus imaged, and the signal read out is radiofrequency, not thermal.
A rotating x-ray beam passes through tissue; detectors measure how much of it is absorbed
That is computed tomography, which is why it uses ionizing radiation and this does not.

set2.io: Objective g — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with contrast administration
set2.q: What is contrast material most commonly used for?
opts: Imaging lung parenchyma, and delineating and characterising interstitial change
Interstitial lung disease is not a stated indication for contrast administration.
Imaging joint cartilage, and delineating and characterising degenerative change
Contrast can be injected into joints, but this is not its commonest use.
Imaging arteries or veins, and delineating and characterising masses
Correct — neoplastic versus benign, and abscess versus cyst, are the examples given.
Imaging bone detail, and delineating and characterising fracture lines
Bone is well seen without contrast, which is not what the deck describes.

set2.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: How do computed tomography angiography and magnetic resonance angiography differ in their use of dye?
opts: Neither injects dye, because both reconstruct the vessels from the raw data afterwards
The computed tomography study does require a rapid iodinated injection.
Computed tomography angiography injects iodine quickly; magnetic resonance angiography needs no dye
Correct — magnetic resonance angiography images the arterial walls without contrast.
Computed tomography angiography needs no dye; magnetic resonance angiography injects gadolinium quickly
This reverses them; the iodinated injection belongs to the computed tomography study.
Both inject iodine, but computed tomography angiography uses a much lower concentration
Magnetic resonance angiography is performed without contrast, so both do not inject.

set2.io: Objective h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set2.q: Which oral contrast agent is contraindicated when perforation is suspected, and what is used instead?
opts: Barium is contraindicated because it is toxic to extra-intestinal tissue; use gastrografin
Correct — barium outside the bowel causes alkaline burns.
Gastrografin is contraindicated because it is toxic to extra-intestinal tissue; use barium
This reverses them; gastrografin is the agent chosen when perforation is possible.
Iohexol is contraindicated because it is toxic to extra-intestinal tissue; use barium
Iohexol is the intravascular agent and is not the oral contrast in question.
Both are contraindicated because either is toxic to extra-intestinal tissue; use none
Gastrografin exists precisely so that a study can still be done.

set2.io: Objective h — Discuss contraindications and safety considerations of commonly used imaging modalities
set2.q: Which patients are described as high risk before contrast administration?
opts: Patients with a documented history of asthma or of seasonal allergic rhinitis
Atopy generally is not the specific high-risk marker the deck gives.
Patients with a documented anaphylactic reaction to any medication
Correct — the history that matters is anaphylaxis to anything, not to iodine alone.
Patients with a documented allergy to shellfish or to dietary iodine
The deck states there should be no cross-reactivity from shellfish.
Patients with a documented reaction to any topical antiseptic containing iodine
Topical iodine reactions are not the risk marker named.

set2.io: Objective f — Compare and contrast the risks and benefits associated with radiation exposure
set2.q: Which disadvantages are named for conventional radiography?
opts: Long scan times and safety problems with magnetic implanted devices
Those are the disadvantages of magnetic resonance imaging.
Very high radiation dose and an inability to be made portable at all
The dose is described as relatively low and the machines can be portable.
A limited range of densities and reliance on ionizing radiation, though at relatively low dose
Correct — the dose is low compared with other radiographic modalities.
Operator dependence and an inability to penetrate bone or large gas-filled structures
Those are the disadvantages of ultrasound.

set2.io: Objective c — Discuss anatomical structures best visualized by each imaging modality
set2.q: Which enteric pathologies is the abdominal series named as evaluating?
opts: Peptic ulceration, gastritis and oesophageal stricture
Luminal mucosal disease is assessed with oral contrast rather than a plain series.
Small bowel obstruction, perforation and volvulus
Correct — the three named examples of enteric pathology.
Appendicitis, diverticulitis and inflammatory bowel disease
These are not the examples the deck gives for the plain abdominal series.
Cholelithiasis, pancreatitis and hepatic abscess
These hepatobiliary conditions are not named for this study.

set2.io: Objective i — Discuss the importance of communication between the physician assistant and radiology team
set2.q: Why does the deck stress giving the radiologist relevant clinical information?
opts: The radiologist repeats the study otherwise, so the history prevents duplicate imaging
Avoiding repeat imaging is described as a benefit of post-processing instead.
The radiologist has not seen the patient, so the history is what guides their read
Correct — the report is only as good as the question it is answering.
The radiologist bills separately, so the indication must be documented for the claim
Billing is not the reason the deck gives for communicating.
The radiologist selects the modality, so the history determines which scanner is booked
They can guide the choice, but the reason stated here is the quality of the read.

set2.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: What does single photon emission computed tomography measure, and what does it show?
opts: Reflected sound on a hand-held transducer, giving real-time images of moving structures
Reflected sound in real time is ultrasonography, which injects no tracer.
Attenuated x-rays on a rotating detector ring, giving cross-sectional images by density
Attenuation by density is computed tomography, which measures the beam it transmits.
Single photons on rotating gamma cameras, giving three-dimensional images of where blood flows
Correct — the deck's stated indication is seeing where blood flows to.
Paired positrons on a stationary gamma camera, giving two-dimensional images of glucose uptake
Positrons and glucose uptake are positron emission tomography, not this study.

set2.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: On a T2-weighted image, how does tissue with high water content appear?
opts: Bright, and the examples given are fat, oedema, infection, blood and cerebrospinal fluid
Correct — remember T2 as the sequence where water is white.
Dark, and the examples given are fat, oedema, infection, blood and cerebrospinal fluid
That is the T1-weighted image; the same list simply inverts between the two.
Bright, and the examples given are cortical bone, tendon, ligament and calcified plaque
Those are low in water and in signal, and calcium emits no signal at all.
Dark, and the examples given are cortical bone, tendon, ligament and calcified plaque
This is true of those tissues but does not answer what high water content does.

set2.io: Objective a — Identify the fundamental properties of medical imaging
set2.q: Which four questions frame the choice of an imaging modality?
opts: Which modality is cheapest, which is fastest, which is closest, and which the patient prefers
Cost and availability matter but are not the framing questions given.
Which modality the radiologist prefers, which is available today, which the insurer covers, and which is quickest
Those are practical constraints rather than the diagnostic framing.
Which modality gives the highest resolution, the largest field of view, the thinnest slices, and the fastest overall scan time for the patient
Technical parameters are not the framing questions given.
Which modality best rules the diagnosis in or out, is there a lower-radiation alternative, what is the risk against benefit for this patient, and is contrast needed
Correct — those are the four the lecture opens with.

set2.io: Objective d — Compare and contrast the concepts of radiographic density and contrast
set2.q: What is the window in computed tomography?
opts: The range of Hounsfield numbers pre-selected for display, spread over the available grey scale
Correct — for example only those densities between −100 and +300.
The physical aperture of the gantry through which the patient passes
That is the bore rather than the window.
The interval during which the contrast sits at its peak concentration in the vessel
That is a timing concept rather than the display window.
The slice thickness selected before the scan is acquired
Slice thickness is a separate acquisition parameter.

set2.io: Objective b — Describe the function and clinical applications of radiography, ultrasonography, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, magnetic resonance angiography, positron emission tomography, single photon emission computed tomography and angiographic studies
set2.q: What is a positron?
opts: An isotope of roughly the same behaviour as technetium, but with a much shorter half-life
A positron is a subatomic particle, not an isotope of any element.
A particle of roughly the same mass as an electron, but carrying the opposite, positive charge
Correct — that is the deck's definition, and the reason for the name.
A photon of roughly the same energy as an x-ray, but emitted by the patient rather than a tube
The emission is a particle rather than a photon; single photons are the other study.
A proton of roughly the same mass as a neutron, but bound within an unstable atomic nucleus
A positron is far lighter than a proton and is not a nuclear constituent.
